paras: The threatened lynching of Smith Wallace was reported from Loveland, Ohio, on November 1, 1888: talk of hanging him followed his preliminary hearing on a charge of attempted rape. Wallace was not harmed; he was bound over to the grand jury and lodged in the Clermont County jail at Batavia, and the only report credited "cool heads" with preventing a lynching.

Wallace had a preliminary hearing before Mayor Clinton of Loveland on a charge of attempted rape, and the mayor bound him over to the grand jury in $1,000 bail. Marshal Martin then took him to Batavia and lodged him in the county jail. According to the report, "the sentiment in favor of lynching ran high," and Wallace "would have been swung up in the wagon bridge" had the counsel of cool heads not prevailed.

The account names neither the accuser nor the date of the alleged offense, and it does not give Wallace's race. It describes no crowd gathering and no move against the jail, only the mood in the town.
No report of an indictment or trial on the attempted-rape charge appears in the coverage.

The case appeared as a single paragraph in the "Ohio Flashes" column of The Stark County Democrat of Canton on November 1, 1888, set among unrelated items on voter registration, deaths and fires. The item stated the charge without qualification and treated the averted hanging as a matter of course, offering no comment on the lynching sentiment beyond crediting the "cool heads" who restrained it. No other paper's report of the case was found.

Wallace was not killed; A1 describes only lynching sentiment that cool heads restrained, after he was bound over and jailed at Batavia, so the case is at most a threatened lynching.
One brief item in a state news column (A1) is the only report found; no local, wire or follow-up account was found.
